articles.title_orig: What to know about Taiwan’s local elections and why they matter to China
articles.title_zh: What to know about Taiwan’s local elections and why they matter to China
articles.content_orig:
TAIPEI, Taiwan (AP) — Taiwan will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties Saturday, in elections focused largely on local issues but also drawing attention from China , which claims the self-governed island as its territory.
The elections are held once every four years, and will be tightly contested between the ruling Democratic Progressive Party and the Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT.
While some experts have in the past compared Taiwan's local elections with the U.S. midterms, as a referendum on the ruling party and its policies, this election cycle has largely focused on bread and butter local issues, without much talk about the island's relationship with China .
Here's what to know about these elections.
From Tainan to Taipei, voters will be choosing between candidates from the DPP and KMT. A third party, the Taiwan People's Party, is also running in some smaller races, and linking up with the KMT in the Taipei mayoral race to support the KMT candidate.
While in the past, the DPP has often used the narrative of defending Taiwan against China's threat in local races, little of that was on display this time, experts said. They also noted less aggressive campaigning this time from candidates who were instead more focused on policy issues.
"Many of the candidates, they toned down their attacks, and in order to try and get the swing voters, they talked more about policy," said Wei-hao Huang, a political science professor at National Sun Yat-sen University.
"How much does the CCP have in actual importance in Taiwan's local elections? Not much," he said, referring to the Chinese Communist Party.
For instance, one issue that has come up nationally has been the installation of solar panels in water reservoirs. The KMT has criticized DPP plans for these as potentially harming water quality.
Although the elections are across the island, none of the contested positions are in the central government.
Experts say that on domestic issues, the government has held fairly steady, ensuring there are social welfare benefits. Despite partisan opposition that has led to political gridlock, citizens may not feel the impact in their day-to-day life.
"In the election period, people won't talk directly about how the central government has performed. One of the reasons is because it seems like (President) Lai Ching-te's approval ratings have been pretty good," said Jia-wei Liu, a professor in the department of public administration and policy at National Taipei University.
Traditionally, the KMT has performed better in local elections. In the last round of local elections in 2022, the DPP won in only 5 out of 22 localities. Experts say the ruling party has only room to grow.
"They have nothing to lose for this election," Sanho Chung, an assistant professor of political science at National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan, said. "They will probably be in a better position than they were before."
Some of the most closely watched races are the mayoral races for Taipei, New Taipei City and Kaohsiung, some of the island's biggest cities. New Taipei City's incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung's mayoral office is held by the DPP.
All three races are tightly contested, Liu said, with candidates basically neck and neck.
Taipei's mayoral race is among the most closely watched. The incumbent mayor, the KMT's Chiang Wan-an, has struggled to garner the level of local support expected of him, Chung said.
The performance of the other Taipei mayoral candidate, Puma Shen, may also have significant implications for the ruling DPP.
Shen has in the past been very vocal about his strong pro-Taiwan independence stance, declaring that Taiwan is an independent country from China. If elected mayor, Liu said, "he'll become a very important political figure in the DPP, and he'd push the party's position more towards independence."
Looming over Taiwan's elections are Chinese influence attempts , which have included efforts to sow distrust in the electoral system.
Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council on Monday again warned the public to be conscious of any disinformation manipulations ahead of the elections, saying that China's artificial intelligence tech had made its methods of infiltration increasingly sophisticated.
The deputy head of the council, Shen Yu-chung, pointed to a recent case where prosecutors were bringing charges against a TPP city council candidate for allegedly taking photos of Taiwanese people and using their faces to create fake accounts for online support, with assistance from China.
Chung said China has a very strong incentive to influence any kind of political outcome in Taiwan, and this incentive has not weakened in this election. However, Taiwan has also learned to adapt, he said.
"They have been developing some antibodies on the disinformation attempts and also other kinds of infiltration attempts," Chung said, pointing to arrests over suspected breaches of the anti-infiltration act.
AP writer Kanis Leung contributed to this report from Hong Kong.

articles.title_orig: US unveils tariffs on EU, China and others over ‘unfair’ trade
articles.title_zh: US unveils tariffs on EU, China and others over ‘unfair’ trade
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies , including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.
The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March , weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump 's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.
The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.
The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.
The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."
An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."
The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.
Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service .
Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."
The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.
Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.
An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

articles.title_orig: The Other Nvidia Romance With an Executive at a Company Linked to China
articles.title_zh: The Other Nvidia Romance With an Executive at a Company Linked to China
articles.content_orig:
A little-known figure in the palace intrigue involving Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and possible chip smuggling is rapidly gaining attention. Ying Cenly Chen, a former senior executive at Super Micro Computer , is alleged to have managed a significant portion of the company’s purchases of Nvidia chips during the period when Supermicro’s hardware was allegedly diverted to China, according to a lawsuit. Her new company, ChronoScale, where Chen serves as CEO, has business ties to both Supermicro and Nvidia.
Chen matters because of her position at Supermicro and because of when she left. A shareholder lawsuit claims that Chen, 50, controlled Supermicro’s supply of Nvidia chips and could not have been unaware of the company’s alleged illicit sales. She exited Supermicro within weeks of an indictment that named Supermicro co-founder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw in the smuggling scheme. She is also married to Ajay “Jay” Puri, Nvidia’s longtime sales chief, Chen confirmed to Fortune . Puri worked for the chipmaker for two decades before announcing his retirement in June.
That means Chen could hold some answers to the question now looming large above Nvidia, which is whether Huang, who resigned as CEO on Nov. 11, knew or turned a blind eye as its chips were potentially diverted to China. And it puts a spotlight on her role at ChronoScale, which develops datacenters that rely heavily on Nvidia chips.
Chen disputes the lawsuit’s account. In emails to Fortune , she said controlling customer allocations of Nvidia chips “was not part of my job responsibility” when she worked at Supermicro. Supermicro also denied that she controlled how its supply of Nvidia GPUs were distributed.
Chen also said she agreed to join ChronoScale before the Supermicro smuggling scandal broke. She told Fortune she accepted the offer on March 10 via DocuSign , nine days before the Liaw indictment was unsealed on March 19. She said the “offer documentation was completed on April 24” and her last day at Supermicro was April 30. That timing would mean Chen remained as chief growth officer at Supermicro for seven weeks after she said she accepted the ChronoScale job, and for six weeks after the indictment.
Liaw, the Supermicro cofounder, was arrested and indicted with two others in a sweeping $2.5 billion smuggling case in March. Liaw has pleaded not guilty; one of his codefendants, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, has pleaded guilty. On a May 5 earnings call , days after Chen’s departure, Supermicro CEO Charles Liang told analysts that “no one” at the company other than the three who had been indicted were involved in the alleged scheme. That declaration, which stunned some observers, came while the Supermicro board was still engaged in an ongoing investigation directors launched following Liaw’s arrest. Under typical circumstances, Liang as CEO and co-founder who knew Liaw for three decades, wouldn’t have been closely involved in an independent board-led investigation, particularly one that was ongoing at the time.
Neither Liang nor Supermicro have been named as targets in the alleged scheme, and Supermicro has said it is itself a victim and is cooperating with authorities. ChronoScale has also not been named by regulators as the target of any investigation. Puri and Nvidia declined to comment. A Supermicro spokesperson denied that Chen controlled how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers and said that after 18 years at Supermicro, Chen “voluntarily resigned in early 2026 to take the CEO role at ChronoScale.”
It wasn’t until August that the Supermicro board’s investigation officially concluded with a finding that the investigation team “did not find any evidence that any current member of senior management had knowledge” about the alleged scheme. By that time, Chen had landed as CEO of ChronoScale, an AI cloud company based in Silicon Valley formed on May 5, 2026, when data-center developer Applied Digital merged its GPU cloud subsidiary, Applied Digital Cloud, into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a Nasdaq-listed maker of robotic exoskeletons. The combined company renamed itself ChronoScale and Applied Digital owns about 96% of it.
Now, a shareholder complaint filed in October has cast a cloud over Chen herself. In a complaint filed Oct. 9 in federal court in San Francisco, former Supermicro employees who are not named allege that Chen controlled Supermicro’s supply of Nvidia chips and that she left because of the U.S. government’s smuggling investigation. Chen is not a defendant in the lawsuit, she has not been charged or accused of wrongdoing by any government agency, and the allegations are unproven.
The lawsuit is a securities class action brought by investors who say Supermicro, Liang and other executives misled them about company sales and export compliance while servers were being allegedly diverted illegally to China, and that they lost money when the March indictment by federal prosecutors in Manhattan sent the stock tanking.
Chen worked at Supermicro from March 2008 to April 2026 and was most recently its chief growth officer and a senior vice president, according to ChronoScale’s filings. According to Chronoscale’s website, she graduated with a Bachelor’s Degree in Science from Fudan University, a public university in Shanghai. The shareholder complaint describes her as a force inside Supermicro who “reported directly to” Liang and led a sales team that it says accounted for “approximately 80% of the company’s total sales.”
One former employee quoted in the lawsuit, described as a Supermicro sales director from July 2023 to July 2025, said Chen “had a very close relationship with Nvidia and managed the company’s acquisition of GPU chips from Nvidia.” Because the supply was limited and in such demand, the former employee said Nvidia “would allocate a certain number to Super Micro, and Chen decided how to distribute them among Super Micro’s customers.” Chen met routinely with Liang “to obtain Liang’s approval of how the chips would be allocated,” according to the complaint.
Supermicro disputes this allegation. “Cenly Chen did not control how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers,” the spokesperson said.
A second former employee in the lawsuit, described as a sales director who worked at Supermicro until 2024, said Chen “handled all allocations of Nvidia chips to Super Micro” and had taken over responsibility for the sales team that covered China. The person said “there was no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge of the company’s illicit sales.”
The complaint also offers an account of why Chen left. The first former employee claimed that Chen’s emails had created a potentially problematic paper trail: “It was widely known within the company that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China.” Citing the former employee, the complaint also states she “resigned so that the company could claim that no current employees were involved in the scheme for which Liaw was arrested.”
Chen disputes the account.
“I do not believe this email exists, as I would never knowingly do such a thing and I don’t believe I ever did,” Chen told Fortune . Both former employees had left Supermicro before Chen did, according to the complaint’s own description of their tenures, and it does not say how they learned the circumstances of her departure.
ChronoScale was created on May 5, when Applied Digital’s cloud business merged into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a public company. Chen’s hiring was not disclosed in securities filings before then. The offer letter ChronoScale filed with the SEC is dated May 5 and shows Chen’s acceptance dated April 24.

articles.title_orig: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record
articles.title_zh: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record
articles.content_orig:
The Spanish Canary Islands witnessed a one-day migration record on Tuesday, with over 2,100 people arriving to the region in over 24 hours.
Most of the migrants landed on the the island of El Hierro, according to Spanish authorities.
"The Canaries can't take it anymore. We're experiencing an unprecedented migration pressure," President of the Canary Islands Fernando Clavijo wrote on X. He requested an urgent meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss an immediate EU response.
Around 100 minors arrived on Tuesday, with a baby also born during the trip from Africa to the islands.
The Canaries, a tourist destination whose shortest gap with northwest Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), tends to see more migrant arrivals in the fall when the waters are calmer. The waters become rougher in the winter due to storms and swells.
Earlier this month, nearly 1,600 migrants from West Africa were saved and taken to the Canary Islands in a previous record. Over 26,000 migrants came to the Canaries this year so far — with half of that figure in November alone.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The route from Africa to the Canaries is one of the deadliest in the world for migrants.
Boats taking off for the islands sometimes drift out to open sea, with the migrants onboard facing starvation, dehydration and lack of medical care. Human smugglers frequently organize the trips and abuse the migrants.
The spike in migration to the Canaries comes as Spain will hold a snap election on Sunday.
Migration, along with housing, will be one of the topics at the forefront of voters' minds when they cast their ballots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who belongs to the center-left Socialist Party, has faced backlash from the opposition regarding his tolerant attitude towards migration. The Spanish government earlier this year enacted a plan to legalize up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In late July, over 80,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta, triggering a crisis for the Sanchez government. Countries such as Germany and Italy tightened or extended border controls due to the influx of migrants into Ceuta.
The far-right Vox party, which could receive its best-ever result in upcoming election, has called for Sanchez and his ministers to be prosecuted for treason over the Ceuta crisis. The conservative Popular Party could form a coalition government with Vox after the election.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck
articles.title_zh: Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian forces have hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.
Ukraine struck the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region, the General Staff said on Wednesday, adding that three MiG-31 jets were used to fire hypersonic missiles and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were damaged.
Russia did not immediately comment on the report by the General Staff, which said the Savasleyka airbase had been hit in the latest long-range attacks aimed at crippling Moscow’s war effort .
The operation followed a series of high-profile strikes by Ukrainian forces in recent days in which two Russian ships were hit in Libyan waters and a Russian vessel was struck in the Gulf of Finland .
Last week, Ukraine destroyed the road portion of Russia’s prized bridge to the Crimea peninsula after consecutive attacks.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end what has become Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
Kyiv is trying to dent Moscow’s military might as it struggles under a renewed campaign of attacks on its energy system and mounting Russian strikes on front-line cities.
Ukrainian forces are hunting Russian ballistic-missile launchers used to carry out many of those attacks, striking 16 over the past several months, Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said this week.
Renewed Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ processing volumes by 45 percent since late October, industry sources said this month. Kyiv has said it will stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow does the same.

articles.title_orig: S. Korea's spy agency denies report about China's alleged proposal for anti-US operations
articles.title_zh: S. Korea's spy agency denies report about China's alleged proposal for anti-US operations
articles.content_orig:
Published : Nov. 26, 2026 - 10:24:22
Add The Korea Herald on Google
South Korea's spy agency has denied a media report that Beijing had proposed covert operations against the United States when the agency sought to secure the release of two informants detained by China early this year.
The Kukmin Daily reported Wednesday that China made the proposal to the National Intelligence Service for the anti-US operations, and that Washington strongly protested it, apparently leading to a chasm in the South Korea-US intelligence partnership.
"The NIS has never received any such proposal from the Chinese authorities," it said in a press notice.
The agency also said intelligence cooperation between Seoul and Washington is proceeding in a "two-way" and "mutually beneficial" manner across various fields, including counterintelligence.
Concerns about bilateral intelligence collaboration have continued following reports earlier this year that the US partially limited Seoul's access to its satellite-based intelligence on North Korea after Unification Minister Chung Dong-young referred to the North's Kusong area as one of the uranium enrichment sites.
Seoul believes that Chung's reference to the Kusong site is based on "open-source" information, while the US side regards it as a disclosure of confidential US information.
Commenting on intelligence cooperation between Seoul and Washington, a senior US official told Yonhap News Agency last month that the US expects South Korea to "uphold the standards of our decadeslong alliance, in particular concerning matters of intelligence and counterintelligence."
Meanwhile, a South Korean engineer, who previously worked for a Korean firm, has been detained in China for nearly three years following his arrest on espionage charges in December 2023, according to a government source. The person has been suspected of informing the NIS of suspected leaks of South Korean semiconductor technology.
The NIS is believed to have started earnest efforts for the detainee's release after President Lee Jae Myung's administration took office last year.
The agency is said to have even considered negotiating a "swap deal" in the first half of this year, offering information on an illegal intelligence agent, known as a "black" operative, in exchange for its citizen's release. The black operative was reportedly affiliated with a third country, not the US or Japan. (Yonhap)

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu says corruption trial ‘must end’ as court suggests dropping case
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu says corruption trial ‘must end’ as court suggests dropping case
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for an immediate end to his long-running corruption trial after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping a case in which he is accused of bribery.
Netanyahu on Wednesday said the “fabricated cases” against him were falling apart, in a televised statement at the Israeli parliament.
Meanwhile, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s parliamentary bloc voted in favour of conducting an independent investigation into the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival after inconclusive October 27 elections.
Eisenkot, who is Netanyahu’s main rival, has been tasked with forming a government, and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.
“Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family,” Netanyahu said in his speech.
“Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul. Who will give those years back to us?”
“The trial must end immediately,” he added.
During a hearing in Jerusalem on Wednesday regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.
In Case 4000, in which Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction.
That case is considered to be the most serious Netanyahu faces and involves him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.
Netanyahu is alleged to have negotiated with Shaul Elovitch, the controlling shareholder of Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq, to get positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefitting Bezeq.
On Wednesday, Israeli media reported Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman saying that proving the bribery charge in that case faced “considerable difficulties”.
Netanyahu, who has been in power on and off for three decades, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and denounced the cases as a politically motivated plot against him.
He is the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial.
Israel’s Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who was unusually summoned to the hearing on Wednesday, said she would consider the judges’ recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal.
In Case 2000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over an alleged deal with the owner of Yediot Aharonot for favourable coverage in exchange for curbs on rival newspaper Israel Hayom. Judges on Wednesday questioned whether his actions constituted a crime and recommended reconsidering the case.
In Case 1000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over allegedly accepting luxury gifts from wealthy individuals in exchange for favours. Judges recommended reaching an agreement to conclude the case.
Netanyahu’s right-wing allies cheered the court’s recommendations and demanded the trial be brought to an end.
“After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset,” Israel Katz, who is the defence minister in Netanyahu’s caretaker government, wrote on X.
Netanyahu’s corruption trial opened in May 2020.
During his most recent term, which started in late 2022, Netanyahu proposed far-reaching judicial reforms that critics say sought to weaken the courts.
With coalition negotiations under way, Eisenkot’s camp is already trying to start unravelling some of the Netanyahu-era judicial reforms in parliament.
The presidential contender is expected to meet Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday evening.
His centrist Yashar party said a day earlier that it had agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
Lieberman has ruled out forming a coalition with Arab-led parties that could hand them a majority in parliament. That has frustrated Democrats chief Yair Golan, who has been pushing Eisenkot to reach a deal with parties representing Israel’s 21 percent Arab minority to make good on his campaign promise to bring down Netanyahu.
The Israeli parliament’s preliminary approval on Wednesday of a probe into the country’s failures prior to the October 7 attack dealt a blow to Netanyahu, who has repeatedly opposed the move.
The vote was the first of four needed ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠to pass a law establishing a state commission to investigate the Hamas attack.
The parliament also voted in favour of a bill seeking to impose term limits on prime ministers and restrict them from serving while under criminal indictment, seemingly taking aim at Netanyahu.
Eisenkot also faced a new challenge on Tuesday after the left-wing Democrats suspended coalition talks, further complicating his potential path to power.
The Yashar party leader has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

articles.title_orig: Xi unleashes China ‘earthquake’ with shock ouster of rising star
articles.title_zh: Xi unleashes China ‘earthquake’ with shock ouster of rising star
articles.content_orig:
He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.
The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.
Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.
He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.
But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.
“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.
Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”
Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.
Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.
In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.
By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.
Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.
“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.
The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.
“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.
“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.
The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.
Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.
Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.
After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.
Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography .
He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring .
The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest , a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.
The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.
Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013.
There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year.
Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook.
Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi.
While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials.
“If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said.
Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China.
“Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.
Max Burman is deputy editor in the London bureau of NBC News Digital.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
CEO Elon Musk will personally match the number of shares the company donates, consistent with his earlier pledge to give one SpaceX share to every kid in America, the company said.
Earlier in the day, the Federal Communications Commission granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed as orbital data centers.
Shares of Rocket Lab Corp (RKLB), AST SpaceMobile, Intuitive Machines also turned green after opening lower on Wednesday.
Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) pared losses on Wednesday and closed higher after falling as much as 9% intraday as investors weighed a fresh company pledge to distribute stock to American children alongside a major regulatory green light for orbital computing.
SPCX shares opened 6% lower on Wednesday and dropped further before paring losses and closing 1.30% higher.

SpaceX said on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued Class A share to every currently active Trump Account, the tax-advantaged investment accounts created for American children.
CEO Elon Musk will personally match the number of shares the company donates, consistent with his earlier pledge to give one SpaceX share to every kid in America. President and COO Gwynne Shotwell separately announced a personal gift of more than 2 million shares.
The company framed the move as extending ownership to the next generation. The corporate portion involves newly issued shares, while Musk's and Shotwell's contributions come from personal holdings and do not increase the share count.
Earlier in the day, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) also granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed as orbital data centers. It is the first U.S. authorization of its kind. The solar-powered modules would process data in space for use on Earth, using optical links supplemented by radiofrequency communications.
Chairman Brendan Carr described the decision as opening a new frontier for computing infrastructure to support U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence. Musk called the approval "a great asset to America and the world."
SpaceX has until late 2033 for its first operational satellite, until 2035 for 100,000 satellites, and until 2040 for the full constellation.
Shares of Rocket Lab Corp (RKLB), AST Spacemobile, Intuitive Machines also turned green after opening lower on Wednesday. While RKLB closed up 2% after opening down 5%, ASTS ended the day 10% higher after briefly touching a fresh 52-week low. LUNR, meanwhile, closed up 2%, after falling as much as 10% intraday.
Rocket Lab is now targeting no earlier than 27 November 2026 for its next Electron launch, a mission named "Night Owls Never Sleep" that will deploy Synspective's 14th StriX synthetic-aperture radar satellite. The flight will be Rocket Lab's 101st Electron launch overall and its 14th for the Japanese Earth-observation company. Rocket Lab remains Synspective's sole launch provider and has another 33 Electron missions under contract with the customer through 2031, even as the company develops its Neutron launch vehicle.
Meanwhile, airspace coordination materials from Caribbean and South American air traffic management this week list a tentative 20 February 2027 date for Blue Origin's New Glenn 5 flight, which AST SpaceMobile's prior commentary have associated with its satellites BlueBirds 17, 18 and19. Blue Origin has yet to confirm the launch date. Previously, the three satellites launch was slated for the first quarter of 2027, without a specific launch date.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around SPCX stock jumped from 'neutral' to 'bullish' territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume stayed at 'normal' levels.
Meanwhile, sentiment around the Tema Space Innovators ETF (NASA) stayed within the 'extremely bullish' territory accompanied by 'high' levels of retail chatter.
SPCX stock closed on Wednesday at about $127, below its June IPO price of $135.

articles.title_zh: South Korea's Kospi leads gains as tech rebound lifts Asia markets
articles.content_orig:
Asia-Pacific markets rose Thursday, tracking Wall Street gains overnight, with tech stocks rebounding from steep losses in the prior session.
South Korea's Kospi gained 1.73%, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 2.32% after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates by an expected 25 basis points, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy.
The central bank raised rates to 3.25%, a 2-year high, in its final meeting of the year, data on the Bank of Korea's website showed .
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.21% in early trade, while the Topix edged 0.71% higher. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.15%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index rose 1.46% while mainland China's CSI 300 added 0.12%.
Asian technology stocks rebounded sharply Thursday, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
SoftBank Group surged more than 11%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 7.3%. Lasertec and Disco both gained more than 6%, while Tokyo Electron climbed 4.6%.
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 4% and 2.1%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Investors appears to have looked past a fresh set of U.S. tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday, targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
Meanwhile, fresh U.S. inflation data reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Overnight in the U.S., the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday, advancing 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite , however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday.

articles.title_orig: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
articles.title_zh: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.
Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.
Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.
In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.
Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
A senior attorney with Earthjustice, Jan Hasselman, criticized the FCC for issuing its decision on a holiday week, and approving the SpaceX proposal without any environmental review, which he said was required by the National Environmental Policy Act.
The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

articles.title_orig: Russia has passed the biggest military budget since Soviet times
articles.title_zh: Russia has passed the biggest military budget since Soviet times
articles.content_orig:
Russia’s State Duma has passed the third reading of a federal budget bill for 2027–2029 that allocates over 50 trillion rubles (approximately $609 billion) to defense, according to the Russian parliament’s official television channel, Duma TV , as reported by Militarnyi .
Under the State Duma Defense Committee’s conclusion on draft law No. 615-9, Russia plans to spend 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.8 billion) on defense in 2027, marking an increase of roughly one-third compared to the 12.93 trillion rubles ($157.4 billion) allocated for 2026 in the previous budget plan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the next three years, total funding for national defense will reach 50.05 trillion rubles ($609.3 billion). Specifically, Moscow plans to allocate 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.8 billion, or 6.91% of GDP) in 2027, 16.61 trillion rubles ($202.2 billion, or 6.3% of GDP) in 2028, and 16.30 trillion rubles ($198.4 billion, or 5.79% of GDP) in 2029. These figures include both public and classified budget expenditures under the “National Defense” category.
Compared to the previous three-year budget plan, defense funding has been increased by 3.58 trillion rubles ($43.6 billion) for 2027 and by 3.56 trillion rubles ($43.3 billion) for 2028.
Overall, total spending for Russia’s federal budget in 2027 is set at 48.74 trillion rubles ($593.3 billion). Direct spending on national defense will account for roughly 35.2% of all federal expenditures, not including additional funding for security and law enforcement agencies listed under other budget sections.
In total, national defense spending in the 2027–2029 budget exceeds the previous three-year budget plan by approximately 10.5 trillion rubles ($127.8 billion).
According to The Moscow Times , this surge in military expenditures will be accompanied by funding cuts across several civilian sectors. Compared to the 2026 figures outlined in the prior budget plan, spending on the national economy will drop by roughly 3%, housing and communal services by 8%, healthcare by 3%, and social policy by 6%.
Russia’s federal budget deficit for 2027 is projected at 5.44 trillion rubles ($66.2 billion), or 2.2% of GDP, with government borrowing expected to serve as the primary source for covering the shortfall.
Previously, it was reported that Russia’s Central Bank has been selling gold from its reserves for ten consecutive months to help cover a widening federal budget deficit, projected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles ($81.1 billion) this year, twice the amount initially anticipated.
The latest reduction brought the country’s total gold reserves to 72.8 million ounces, their lowest level since late 2019.
The State Duma is the lower house of Russia's parliament, the Federal Assembly, responsible for drafting and passing federal laws along with approving certain government appointments.

articles.title_orig: In a First, Earth Has Stretch of 6 Days Over Warming Ceiling
articles.title_zh: In a First, Earth Has Stretch of 6 Days Over Warming Ceiling
articles.content_orig:
Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever on record
With the most powerful El Niño in living memory still gaining strength, this record could soon be surpassed
By Andrea Thompson edited by Claire Cameron
Amanda Montañez; Source: Copernicus Climate Change Service ( data )
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever measured on the planet. According to preliminary data from the Europe-based Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), Friday, November 20, 2026, was 2.12 degrees Celsius higher than the preindustrial average—or the time before humans began heating up Earth by burning fossil fuels.
The record stems from a combination of long-term, human-driven climate change and a blockbuster El Niño that is likely the strongest in the past 1,000 years. It comes as international negotiations at the COP31 climate summit have fallen apart, with no global agreement on how to rein in global warming.
Amanda Montañez; Source: Copernicus Climate Change Service ( data )
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There are likely to be more days with an anomaly at or above 2 degrees C as this El Niño builds to its crescendo over roughly the next month. The next several months are also likely to be record hot. “I think we will likely see more days exceeding 2 degrees C over the next couple of months (possibly through March 2027),” says Zachary Labe, a scientist at Climate Central, a climate research nonprofit, “though I still expect this to be more a rarity than the norm when comparing every day.”
It’s possible 2026 will be the hottest year on record, besting 2024, though it will be close and could end in a tie. Because it takes time for the heat released by El Niño in the Pacific to affect global temperatures, 2027 will likely see the biggest heat effect and will almost certainly become the hottest year on record. Both 2026 and 2027 are expected to be more than 1.5 degrees C above preindustrial temperatures, a level so far only ever surpassed in 2024.
Under the landmark 2015 Paris climate agreement , which came out of the COP21 meeting, countries agreed to limit warming to “well below” 2 degrees C above preindustrial and to try to keep it under 1.5 degrees C. But the United Nations recently announced that the world will blow past the 1.5 degrees C mark , with global temperatures expected to hit 1.8 degrees C above preindustrial.
Surpassing the 2 degrees C benchmark for a day—or even a year—doesn’t mean the Paris Agreement limit has been permanently breached, because that considers the average temperature over many years. By that measure, the world has warmed by nearly 1.4 degrees C above preindustrial, according to the U.N.
The COP31 summit—to which the U.S. did not send an official delegation—ended without an agreement for a final deal. These documents nominally provide a blueprint for countries to follow in their efforts to lower greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the changing climate.
In a statement, outgoing secretary-general António Guterres, who has been a vocal supporter of phasing out fossil fuels, noted his “profound frustration” at the summit’s outcome. “Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly,” Guterres said. “The world is now poised to exceed the globally-agreed limit of a 1.5 degree temperature rise. The window to keep that overshoot as short and shallow as possible is rapidly closing.”

articles.title_orig: Rockstar is handing out 100 of these gorgeous limited-edition GTA 6 PS5 consoles, and you can't buy one
articles.title_zh: Rockstar is handing out 100 of these gorgeous limited-edition GTA 6 PS5 consoles, and you can't buy one
articles.content_orig:
Over my Thanksgiving holiday, I plan to pick up a couple of square groupers for a shady acquaintance, “borrow” a quad-engine center console without the hassle of asking its owner, beat the traffic in Islamorada with a seaplane, and lead roughly two dozen cops on a high-speed chase. If I happen to mow down a pedestrian or two along the way, it’s nothing a fresh outfit and quick paint job can’t fix.
Probably worth mentioning that I’ll be doing all of this from my couch.
Because, in the perfect words of Kristen Livengood, Monroe County’s public information officer, “I live where you GTA.”
If your teenager or employees decided to make a suspiciously long weekend of it last Thursday and Friday, you’re not alone. Nov. 19 marked the long-awaited release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI, an open-world video game masterpiece more than 13 years in the making.
Originally set for release in fall 2025, a first teaser trailer for the game racked up 93 million views in 24 hours, setting a YouTube record for a non-music video debut. Its second trailer blew the first out of the water, soaring to more than 475 million views. Two delays of the launch date turned the game into an internet meme before release.
But upon first glance, it would appear the wait was well worth it.
Loosely based on South Florida, protagonist Jason Duval begins his story in the fictional “Leonida Keys” – complete with a first mission spent chasing down square groupers thrown from a plane.
Though not officially confirmed by Rockstar, a Reuters report estimated the game’s production budget at more than $1 billion – that’s more than all three “Lord of the Rings” movies combined, if you’re counting – and the painstaking attention to detail in re-creating the Keys shows every cent. From the distressed aesthetic of a classic stilted 3/2 Keys home, to neighborhoods full of Conch homes with chain link fences, Monroe County residents are immediately immersed in a world that looks just about identical to the one outside their doors.
I started to list all of the Keys landmarks that make an appearance, most with slight aesthetic changes or altered names.
But the list soon ran off the page, and it’s more than 200 items long.
The Leonida Keys are a whole lot shorter than real life – a 2.5-hour drive is compressed into about 2 minutes – and even still, icons like Fat Albert the blimp, Fred the Tree on the Seven Mile Bridge, Naval Air Station Key West, Bahia Honda and the unsightly microwave relay tower in Key Largo make the cut.
There are some necessary differences in a game based on crime and free will for the player. I’ve never seen so many Coast Guard boats in my life, and I was a little taken aback when Betsy the giant lobster in Key Largo was replaced by a whale.
Even still, the painstaking attention to detail makes it easy to lose dozens of hours simply exploring just one corner of GTA VI’s map that feels like home. From swinging gear on trap boats to accent lights on boats that change with the time of day and accurate fish species caught off Jason’s dock (I suck just as bad at rod fishing in the game as real life), even my four or five hours spent exploring for this article barely scratched the surface.
Nearly a week in, the rest of the world seems to agree.
Launch day retail sales of GTA VI were a staggering $3.79 billion, according to parent company Take-Two Interactive, which touted the release as the “biggest entertainment launch in history” after outselling the entire theatrical run of “Avatar” in a single day.  The game sold 32.5 million copies before release, with internet service providers bracing themselves for players to download the massive 212 GB file.
Online review aggregator Metacritic scored the game at 99/100 from 152 critic reviews, while facing a more divided user reception based on free will for the protagonist and a lack of a PC edition at launch.
One U.S. Army unit in Georgia even made national news when it offered active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game in return for re-enlistment contracts signed between Aug. 1 and Nov. 13.
For a franchise that made its name on crime, murder and scantily-clad characters, GTA VI picks some odd moral hills to stand on. Players can free Lolita the killer whale from the barely-disguised former Miami Seaquarium, and the game inspired rage from online viewers incensed that Jason can no longer cheat on his girlfriend with sex workers (priorities, people).
But still, the gaming juggernaut has largely lived up to its 13-year wait. Now please excuse me while I get back to my controller.

articles.title_orig: 2 California companies are buying Nvidia's most advanced chips. Those companies are actually Chinese-owned, a CBS News investigation reveals.
articles.title_zh: 2 California companies are buying Nvidia's most advanced chips. Those companies are actually Chinese-owned, a CBS News investigation reveals.
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia is selling its most cutting-edge chips to at least two companies that are U.S.-based, but are actually controlled by Chinese-owned firms, raising fresh questions about efforts to keep sensitive technology away from the nation's rivals, a CBS News investigation found.
One of the chip giant's "preferred partners" is a California company owned by a Chinese firm whose chief executive is a graduate of a Chinese military university, records show. Another California company was renamed after its Chinese-owned parent company was blacklisted.
Some of these U.S.-based, Chinese-owned firms have then leased or sold the advanced chips, used for artificial intelligence, to other companies in Southeast Asia, records show.
The world of computer chip exports is murky — and labyrinthine chains of custody have made it even more difficult to determine just how many of the most sensitive Nvidia chips are being exploited by China, experts told CBS News.
"It is a wake-up call for accountability, for properly resourcing the enforcement bodies, and for every leading private-sector tech company to map where it is exposed," said Mishel Kondi, a senior analyst at C4ADS, which specializes in using public data, from corporate filings to satellite imagery, to uncover sanctions violations and smuggling.
C4ADS, a Washington-based global security nonprofit also known as the Center for Advanced Defense Studies, examined corporate filings and other company ownership data at the request of CBS News. This story is based on dozens of corporate filings, court records and an investigation of Nvidia's corporate relationships dating back to 2023 — long before its CEO Jensen Huang and his behemoth chip company dominated the news cycle.
That explosive saga began 27 days ago when the news broke that Huang had been having an affair with Alice Huang — a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The Justice Department has said it has not reached a conclusion, and Beijing denies she is a spy. The company she ran, Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore, is under investigation by the Justice Department for allegedly circumventing export bans by obtaining computer chips for use by China.
But Megaspeed , national security and trade experts say, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the transfer of Nvidia chips to China. And elected officials are now asking questions like: How are Nvidia's chips getting to China? And what did Jensen Huang and his colleagues know about it?
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement this week.
Nvidia had almost $20 billion in sales to China last year. The company can sell graphics cards for personal computers and server chips with lower processing power to China without a special license.
What is not allowed — and is under strict export controls — are the sales of Nvidia's most technologically advanced chips, which are powering the AI revolution.
But recent reporting, including from CBS News, has shown some of the highest end chips, called Blackwells, have made it into Chinese hands.
The circuitous trail traveled by Nvidia chips quickly gets muddy.
Take RiCloud AI, a data center company based in San Jose, California. RiCloud AI appears on Nvidia's list of "preferred partners" in the U.S., affording it preferential access to sales of high-end computer chips used for advanced AI models.
These are classified as American sales, according to Nvidia's public filings — with the chips going to RiCloud AI, Inc., a U.S. company.
But RiCloud AI's parent company is Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Limited. That company is headquartered in Shenzhen, China, and is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
Yuxing's CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, has a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, a university run by the Chinese military. Yu is also CEO of a related RiCloud company in California.
And Yuxing's chairman, Li Qiang, was previously chairman of data firm Global Switch Holdings, which was dropped as a data center provider by Australia's Department of Defense in June 2024 over national security concerns.
The U.S. government has not accused RiCloud and Yuxing of any wrongdoing.
By December 2025, just 10 weeks after it was incorporated, RiCloud AI had secured its partner status with Nvidia and has since become a "preferred" cloud partner, giving the company priority access to advanced chips, Nvidia's software and technical support. Nvidia has not responded to questions about what background checks it conducted before awarding the privileged status to RiCloud AI.
An examination of RiCloud AI's clients suggests that some seem like unorthodox customers for such high-powered technology. This year, for example, it signed a $120 million deal to lease 300 Nvidia B300 servers to a company in Taiwan that was primarily known for selling whisky.
Agencia Comercial Spirits was a small whisky importer with $609,000 in net income in 2025 when it listed on the Nasdaq as an AI company. This year it has made commitments for AI data center-related deals totaling between $488 and $598 million, after Li was appointed as chairman.
Agencia did not respond to a request for comment. In a February press release announcing its pivot into data centers, Agencia said the move was "part of a broader review of strategic opportunities outside its core whisky business."
Then there is California company Aivres, which is currently listed on Nvidia's website as an "elite" compute partner — the highest tier of relationship with the chip giant.
Aivres used to be called Inspur, the same name as its Chinese parent company. But when Inspur group firms in China were added to a federal blacklist of companies considered a security risk to the U.S. in March 2023, the California subsidiary changed its name and today still maintains its close relationship with Nvidia. Aivres itself is not on the blacklist.
Aivres, which produces data center servers housing Nvidia chips, exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, according to a New York Times analysis of trade records published two months ago.
Some $3 billion of those exports were for computers containing Nvidia's cutting-edge Blackwell chips, which are restricted from being exported to China, the Times reported.
The Aivres chips then went to two companies in Malaysia — Megaspeed and Aolani — providing cloud AI services to Chinese firms Alibaba and ByteDance, according to the Times.
Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm where Jensen Huang paramour Alice Huang was a top executive, was blacklisted by the U.S. government this week, in the wake of the scandal. The company denies any wrongdoing.
The Pentagon put Alibaba on a blacklist in June, claiming it used advanced chips to help the Chinese military. The company denies it and sued the government over the blacklisting, winning a preliminary injunction last month.
The servers owned by Inspur — Aivres' parent company — are used in China by the country's military, according to the U.S. government . Aivres did not respond to requests for comment.
Another of Nvidia's elite U.S. partners has surfaced in a recent $300 million chip smuggling case, though it has not been accused of wrongdoing.
Earlier this year, a California businessman named Greg Lui was indicted for allegedly smuggling export-controlled chips to China via Malaysia and Singapore in 2023 and 2024. He has pleaded not guilty.
Records reviewed by CBS News link Lui to 2CRSi, an Nvidia elite partner in the U.S. that is a branch of a French-owned company making AI data servers.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow closes higher after big comeback; S&P 500, Nasdaq fall but end well off lows — live update
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow closes higher after big comeback; S&P 500, Nasdaq fall but end well off lows — live update
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday as Wall Street tried to recover from steep declines led by artificial intelligence-linked stocks.
The blue-chip Dow advanced 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite , however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.
Stocks came well off their lows as the session went on. The blue-chip Dow lost more than 1,100 points, or 2.2% at its low of the day. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 4.6%, and the broad market S&P 500 shed 3.2% at their respective lows.
Traders chalked up part of the rebound to light trading ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday as well as the circulation of a blog post by Michael Burry, in which he said that his portfolio is " temporarily almost entirely long ."
The Dow was boosted by gains in stocks such as International Business Machines , Salesforce and Sherwin-Williams . S&P 500 sectors such as materials, energy and real estate were all higher, bolstering the index.
However, Nvidia led AI-related stocks lower, dropping almost 4%. Micron Technology moved down 4.5%, while Oracle declined more than 5%, and Alphabet shed more than 2%. The State Street Technology Select Sector ETF (XLK) ended nearly 1% lower.
Meanwhile, semiconductor stock Ambarella plummeted more than 19% after its forecast for the current quarter came in light . The company's earnings and revenue for the third quarter also missed expectations.
"This market is very bifurcated" between AI and non-AI stocks, said David Wagner, head of equities at Aptus Capital Advisors. "The market is pulling back obviously due to a pullback in tech, pullback in semis, pullback in the AI narrative, but right now, I don't see that being a growth scare. I see it being a sentiment-based scare" based on factors such as the composition of Congress in the new year, he added.
To be sure, there's still a "big worry" among investors that the worries in AI could move from a sentiment-based scare to a growth-based scare "if the market starts pricing in too much Fed activity of hiking rates," Wagner also said.
October's personal consumption expenditures price index reading showed that inflation still isn't slowing down, which reiterated expectations for interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve in December and January and put investors in a risk-off mood.
Headline PCE rose 0.3% last month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.8%. While both figures were in line with expectations, the annual rate increased from 3.7% in September. Excluding food and energy prices, core PCE increased 3.3% year over year, coming in slightly above the Dow Jones forecast.
Investor sentiment was also weighed by the White House unveiling a barrage of new tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
Wall Street is coming off a losing session for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, after tech stocks gave back some of their gains from the prior session as Nvidia sank and Anthropic fell below its IPO price.
Tuesday's choppy trading action was just the latest in a volatile month. Even before the ouster and reinstatement of Nvidia's Jensen Huang — which sent stocks soaring Monday — and Democrats' sweep in the midterm elections, investors were deliberating the future of the artificial intelligence build-out amid a worsening macroeconomic outlook.
The U.S. stock market will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving. The market will also close at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended the session in positive territory.
The 30-stock Dow added 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to 50,182.95. On the flip side, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite fell 0.25% and 0.62% to 7,182.78 and 23,585.80, respectively.
The stock market has sharply curtailed its losses, with the S&P 500 now down about 0.3% versus its slump of 3.2% earlier Wednesday.
The stocks that have seen the biggest bounce from their session lows Coherent , Axon Enterprise and Bloom Energy . See below for a few of the names that have also rebounded.
— Darla Mercado and Nick Wells
U.S. consumers plan to spend more this holiday season, with higher-income households driving the increase while lower-income shoppers pulling back, according to a recent Citi survey.
The survey of about 2,500 consumers conducted with Citi's Innovation Lab from Nov. 5 to Nov. 16 showed  that respondents plan to spend 12% more than 2025 holiday season, highlighting the K-shaped consumer theme.
Inflation remained a concern, with 72% of respondents at least somewhat worried about food and fuel prices. Among those cutting spending, 48% said higher food and fuel costs, up from 39% last year. Shoppers reported price increases across all 11 categories surveyed, led by groceries, clothing, electronics, and home improvement.
Higher-income households are driving the gain with households earning more than $100k planning to spend $1,202, up 34%, while those earning under $25,000 expect to spend $295, down 3%.
The divide reflects a reversal from last year, when the highest-income group planned the steepest spending cut (-15%) and the lowest-income group was the only one expecting to spend more (+6%), Citi wrote.
SpaceX has received authorization from the Federal Communications Commission to launch 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites into orbit, leading its shares to rise.
The company's chairman Brendan Carr said Wednesday in an social media post that the approval would help "extend America's lead in Super Intelligence."
Shares of the space company ticked up more than 1% on Wednesday.
Ratings agency S&P Global put Nvidia 's rating on "CreditWatch Negative," pointing to rising risks from the company's management and governance framework.
Nvidia currently has an issuer credit rating of AA.
"Recent well-publicized developments have raised questions about the effectiveness of NVIDIA Corp.'s management and governance framework, including board independence and 'key man' risk," the ratings agency said in a Wednesday announcement .
The artificial intelligence bellwether has been making headlines – and has seen its stock make sharp swings – following the controversial exit and reinstatement of its CEO Jensen Huang. In November alone, shares are down 27%.
" News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in NVIDIA's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," the rating agency said.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) was down more than 2% on Wednesday, adding to its recent losses and pacing for its worst performance over 10 trading sessions in more than a year.
The fund — which shed 7.3% on Tuesday — has fallen more than 17% since the Nov. 11 close. If that holds through Wednesday's close, the fund will record its worst 10-day period since April 2025.
— Nick Wells and Sean Conlon
Michael Burry is "almost entirely long" on stocks, even as various areas of the market continue to sell off, the investor said Wednesday in a recent edition of his newsletter.
"Globally, my portfolio is more long, and less short, than it has been in some time," Burry wrote in the Substack post. "In fact, when I say less short, right now apart from Palantir puts and MetLife puts, I am temporarily almost entirely long. Temporarily, because I am continuing to assess short opportunities."

Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.

articles.title_orig: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
articles.title_zh: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
"News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P said in a Wednesday note .
Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level.
S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed.
A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. Nvidia priced $25 billion of investment-grade senior notes in June, with maturities from 2028 through 2056, shortly after S&P upgraded the company from AA- to AA.
Nvidia has about $32.5 billion of bonds in the U.S. high-grade corporate bond index, according to Bloomberg.
S&P's Wednesday note follows Moody's Ratings changing its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18, citing governance concerns, and leaving that outlook unchanged after Huang's return on Monday.
In its note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a reason their independence may be "compromised" and said Nvidia's management and governance risk was "rising."
The ratings agency added that it remained unaware of any remedial action taken by the board to address what could be "meaningful" management and governance deficiencies.
Chairman Harvey Jones and early investor Tench Coxe have served on Nvidia's board since 1993, while Brooke Seawell joined in 1997. Mark Stevens served from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008.
S&P also flagged questions around geopolitical risk management and internal controls arising from Nvidia's exposure to China.
"While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the "key man" risk to the forefront," S&P's Andrew Chang and David Tsui said.
Chang and Tsui noted that Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement did not resolve questions about the board's oversight of executive conduct.
The agency also intends to meet with Nvidia's board and management to discuss plans to address those deficiencies, particularly around "board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession plan."
Huang returned less than two weeks after Jones said Nvidia's directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back, sending Nvidia shares up as much as 36% during Monday's session.
Nvidia shares are down about 12.5% since Monday's close.
